newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Poll fairness a key test for Algerian leaders.
newsitem.headline: Poll fairness a key test for Algerian leaders.

text.p: The fairness of Algeria's general elections on Thursday is a key test for President Liamine Zeroual's plan to tolerate a rainbow of opposition parties in the new parliament, diplomats and analysts said.

"We have no hope that the election itself will end the violence but we hope that a credible election will be a first step towards political reforms opening the door for more reforms," said a Western diplomat.

About 8,000 candidates from 39 political parties, including the National Democratic Rally (RND) which groups Zeroual's staunch supporters, are running for the 380-seat National Assembly (lower house).
More than 16.7 million people, the majority of them disaffected young people, are eligible to take part in the first parliamentary polls since December 1991.
In the 1991 voting the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), now outlawed, took a commanding lead in the first round and the authorities then scrapped the poll.
Political analysts say the RND and the moderate Islamist-oriented Movement for a Peaceful Solution (MPS) are battling for the largest share of the vote.
But the new system of proportional representation virtually guarantees that at least four or five parties will be represented with no party gaining an absolute majority.
"The worst scenario for the country is a rigged election as the authorities will lose more credibility among the people and political parties," a Western diplomat said.
A rigged election will spread despondency among moderate Islamists and boost the ranks of Moslem guerrillas, locked in a violent campaign to turn Algeria into a purist Islamic state, he said.

"All legal parties will lose their political grass-roots support and people will lose hope in true political opening, and then armed groups could mobilise more followers and the violence will increase in the mid-term," the diplomat said.
Zeroual vowed a fair vote and pledged a neutral stand by the authorities, but political leaders have taken no chances, urging supporters to keep a close eye on ballot boxes.

"You should stand by our side and participate in supervising the poll and the vote counting. We have no trust in the regime," Khalida Massoudi, an Algiers candidate for the anti-Islamist Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD), told supporters at the end of the 19-day-long campaigning on Monday.
MPS leader Mahfoud Nahnah warned the authorities that Algeria would slide into a deeper crisis if voters were cheated.
More than 15,000 party officials are members of polling supervisory committees along with representatives of human rights groups and officials.

"We have no clear indications whether the election will be rigged or not but my government made it clear that the poll's international credibility has a price which is fairness," another Western diplomat said,
Secular opposition Socialist Front (FFS) said if the authorities cheated to boost pro-government RND candidates people would take to the streets and stage violent protests.
Diplomats say the strength of each party varied especially in the countryside where votes could be won according to complicated links with the chiefs of tribes and large families.

Zeroual also faces a test of how he will use his constitutional paramount power to develop understanding and participation between the executive government and the opposition in the constitutionally weak legislative body.

"Without a solution based on consensus and a working relationship between youths, parliament and executive governing branches, the huge gap separating youths and the political community will continue," one diplomat said.
Three quarters of Algeria's 29 million people are under the age of 30. The young are hardest hit by unemployment, running at more than 28 percent of the country's five million workforce.
Diplomats say while the now-outlawed radical FIS has lost much of its once huge political support, some of its leaders can still yield an influence to reduce violence.
"The FIS as an organised party does not exist any more...It seems that the party leaders, even abroad, have no clear vision on how to deal with the authorities," a diplomat said.
Secularist FFS and other parties want Zeroual to open negotiations with the main opposition, including FIS political leaders, to stop bloodshed.

The government, backed by several political groups, says "the FIS file is closed" and rejects any dialogue with radical leaders blaming their fellow rebels for massacres of civilians and other violence in which an estimated 60,000 people have died in the past five and half years.

"If (jailed FIS leader) Ali Belhadj appears on TV to call for an end to bloodshed I personally believe that the level of violence may decrease by between 30 and 50 percent," said a diplomat, adding that this was not on the political agenda yet.
